catalog_quote: 22. Vowels appear to be generally long in penultimate syllables when stressed (for instance, the o's in cibode, tsonga, the i in darika, the first i in murindi, the first a in ngwara); otherwise they are short. In a simple system of transcription such as would be required for a fixed orthography of the language it does not appear necessary to mark the length. IV.—STRESS. 23. The stress is normally on the penultimate syllable of long words, but in rapid speech there sometimes seems to be a rhythmical stress on other syllables. This was noticeable in Mr. Nkomo's pronunciation of the words coani, pingura in the text, where there was a distinct stress on the first syllables when the sentences were pronounced rapidly.

audit.reasoning: Quote verified verbatim at the stated page (p. 10, pars. 22-23; par. 7 pp. 7-8) in the held archive.org scanned and per-page XML of Jones 1911. The deciding source is a primary, first-hand phonetic description by Daniel Jones, but from 1911 and one speaker. No modern grammar or prosodic study of Ndau exists (Glottolog has none; web search finds only a segmental-phonology DPhil 2017, a sociolinguistic PhD 2017, a tone article 1962, and Mkanganwi's 1973 MPhil with a 'preliminary note' on phonology, none open). Held Borland 1970 is silent on stress (tone only). sources.citation: Hyman, Larry M. (2009). Penultimate lengthening in Bantu: analysis and spread. UC Berkeley Phonology Lab Annual Report 2009, 195-209.
sources.quote: Shona (cluster to which Ndau belongs) has predictable penultimate lengthening, word-level half-length plus phrase/utterance-final full length; no Ndau-specific statement.
sources.locator: pp. 195-196 (Shona ex. (1) ku-se:k-a etc.; Shona/Tswana 'half-length' on penult of every word vs full phrasal PL), p. 207 typology table (Shona: no lexical length contrast, + penultimate lengthening)

sources.citation: Doke, Clement M. (1931). Report on the Unification of the Shona Dialects. Hertford: Stephen Austin for the Government of Southern Rhodesia. [ALLEX/Univ. of Oslo 2005 photographic reprint with introduction by H. Chimhundu; fetched sources via Wayback Machine]
sources.quote: Doke: 'the function of stress in Bantu is that of word-building. In each word or word-group in Bantu there is one, and only one, main stress' (basis for conjunctive word division across all Shona groups incl. Ndau). Chimhundu: the Shona word marker 'has been clearly identified by both Doke and Fortune as penultimate length or stress... accent or prominence of extra length (and perhaps extra stress) on the second last syllable... shifts as affixes or inflections are added'.
sources.locator: Report sec. 150, p. 82 (PDF p. 162; scanned); Chimhundu introduction pp. 58-60 (text layer, lines 2203-2290). The Report's 'Outline of Shona Phonetics' (pp. 37-75, scanned) has no length/stress section; Ndau is one of Doke's dialect groups.

sources.citation: Curtis (Burlin), Natalie; Simango, C. Kamba; Cele, Madikane (1920). Songs and tales from the dark continent. New York: G. Schirmer. archive.org id songstalesfromda00burl (scanned text).
sources.quote: 'Ba'ntu African words are usually accented on the penultima... As there are a few exceptions to this general rule, all the accents are here given'; 'Unless otherwise indicated, all words are accented on the penultima'; the Vandau shift accent in singing vs speaking ('The accent of this word is changed in singing from the fourth syllable to the third. This rhythmic shifting of accent is found in many of the Ndau songs'). Speaker: C. Kamba Simango, Ndau of Portuguese East Africa.
sources.locator: Ndau section, pronunciation note before the songs (printed p. 13-14; scanned lines 1281-1282, 1910-1920) and song footnote (scanned line 2570, p. 24)
